1.goal: To open on the gap between writing an opinion and saying one.
run: Ask whether she opened the pre-class and whether anything in it was unclear.
Say what today is, in the words below. Do not name the three moves yet — screen 7 is where she finds them.
Ask the question on screen. Take whatever comes, in either language.
exact: What today is: “Today you hear Maya and Chris talking. Then you keep a conversation going with me, about anything you choose.”
If she has no answer: “What do you say in Portuguese while you are thinking? There is one in English too.”
1.expected: Something about going blank, or about translating first. She may answer in Portuguese and that is fine here.
1.support: Offer two: does she go quiet, or does she say something in Portuguese?
1.challenge: Ask what the other person does while she is thinking.
1.monitoring: Whether she recognizes the problem before the lesson names it.
1.evidence: What she says she does in the silence today. Compare it with what she actually does on screen 10.
1.transition: Move on once she has heard what today is.

2.goal: To place the conversation: same two people, same movie, no time to choose words.
run: Read the brief with her.
Remind her of the two positions from last lesson.
Ask the question: what is harder about saying an opinion out loud than writing it?
2.expected: Time. Writing lets you choose the word; speaking does not. That is the whole answer.
2.support: If nothing comes, ask how long she took over the four sentences in the pre-class, and how long a person waits for an answer.
2.challenge: Ask which of the two she thinks will say more in this conversation, and why.
2.monitoring: Whether she remembers the two positions from last lesson without being told.
2.evidence: How much of lesson 19 survived a week.
2.transition: Move on when the two positions are back on the table.

3.goal: To have her predict the shape of the conversation before hearing it.
3.interaction: T–S, guessing out loud. No confirmation.
run: Read the three questions with her.
Take one guess on each and write them down where she can see them.
Do not confirm anything — the first listening does that.
exact: Before the guesses: “You do not know yet. Guess anyway — we'll check when we listen to the conversation.”
3.expected: Three guesses. The third one — does it end badly — is the interesting one.
3.support: Offer two options on each and let her choose one. Choosing is still risking.
3.challenge: Ask her to predict who says the last line.
3.monitoring: Whether she risks a guess. She tolerates error well, so this should be quick.
3.evidence: Her three predictions, checked on the next screen.
3.transition: Move on as soon as all three have an answer.

4.goal: To understand the situation and the direction of the conversation, once, at normal speed.
run: Say what she is listening for before you press play: who asks whom to explain. Nothing else.
Play once at Normal. Do not stop it, and do not play it twice on this screen.
Take the three answers, and go back to her predictions.
exact: Before pressing play: “We listen once, all the way through. While you listen, find one thing only: which of them asks the other to explain.”
4.expected: Maya asks first, Chris asks at the end. Neither changes their mind. Her predictions are usually right about the first and wrong about the third.
4.support: If she caught nothing, play it once at Slower and ask only the first question.
4.challenge: Ask what the last thing said was, and who said it.
4.monitoring: Whether she listens for the whole or tries to catch every word. This is the listening baseline of the cycle.
4.evidence: How much she got from one pass at normal speed.
4.transition: Move on once the three questions have answers.

5.goal: To rebuild the order of the conversation from a second listening with a new purpose.
5.interaction: S alone on the activity, then T–S to check.
run: Read the six lines with her before you play anything, so she knows what she is looking for.
Play once at Normal. Let her place what she can, then play once more at Slower.
Check the order, and ask what the shape of it is: who does what, in what order.
5.expected: Tell, refuse, ask why, reason, concede, ask back. The reason arrives fourth, and only because somebody asked.
5.support: If she is stuck between two, ask which one has to come before the other for the conversation to make sense.
5.challenge: Ask which line the conversation could not do without.
5.monitoring: What she holds from one listening to the next. This is the listening measure of the lesson.
5.evidence: How many she placed after one pass, and how many after two.
5.transition: Move on when the six are in order and the shape has been named.

6.goal: To hear the three phrases that disappear into one another at speed, and to see that the three plausible ones are not there.
6.interaction: S alone, then T–S, with the audio at the slowest setting.
run: Let her mark the three before playing anything.
Play at Slower, twice if she needs it, and let her change her answers.
Check them. Spend the time on the two that sound like the real ones.
exact: On the pair that sounds alike: “Listen again. Is it ‘why do you say that’ or ‘why do you not like it’? Those are two different questions.”
6.expected: The three real ones are the ones that run together. The three false ones are what a careful reader expects to hear, which is why they are hard.
6.support: Say the false one and the real one back to back yourself, at speed, and ask which one she heard.
6.challenge: Ask her to say I will give you that at speed, the way Chris does.
6.monitoring: Whether she can separate what she heard from what she expected. This is the thing behind most of her listening difficulty.
6.evidence: Which of the three false ones she marked, and whether the slower speed changed her answer.
6.transition: Move on when the three are settled.

7.goal: To name the three moves that keep the conversation open, from lines she has already heard.
run: Let her sort the six lines on her own.
Check them, and ask what each move is for: what would happen without it?
Count them out loud at the end: only two of the six are about the movie.
7.expected: Two of each. The concession is the one people misplace, because it looks like agreement.
7.support: Ask, on each line: does this ask something, buy time, or give something away?
7.challenge: Ask which of the three moves she already does in Portuguese without thinking about it.
7.monitoring: Whether she sees the moves as a system rather than as six separate phrases.
7.evidence: Which move she says is hardest for her. It predicts what she will avoid on screen 10.
7.transition: Move on to production once the six are sorted.

8.goal: To buy time out loud, four times, with four different phrases.
run: Ask the four questions below, one straight after the other, at speed.
She must start every answer with one of the four phrases on screen, and a different one each time.
Speed matters more than content here. Do not stop for anything.
exact: Setting it up: “I ask, you answer. Every answer starts with one of these four — and not the same one twice.”
Question 1: “How was your week at school?”
Question 2: “What are you watching at the moment?”
Question 3: “Are you happy with the subjects you chose this year?”
Question 4: “What are you doing on Saturday?”
8.expected: Four answers, four different openers. The fourth is the hard one, because the easy two are gone.
8.support: Point at the one she has not used yet.
8.challenge: Ask a fifth question and let her choose freely.
8.monitoring: Whether the phrase comes before the silence or after it. Before is the point.
8.evidence: Whether buying time out loud is starting to be automatic, or still needs the screen.
8.transition: Move on once four different openers have been used.

9.goal: To react and then ask back, three times, without waiting for a turn.
9.interaction: T–S. You state opinions; she reacts.
run: State the three opinions below, one at a time.
Each time she does two things: reacts, and asks you why.
Answer her question properly each time. She needs to see the move work.
exact: Setting it up: “I say what I think. You do two things: react, and ask me why. Every time.”
Opinion 1: “Series are better than films. Two hours is not enough to care about anyone.”
Opinion 2: “School should start at ten, not at seven.”
Opinion 3: “Nobody should have to choose a career at sixteen.”
9.expected: Three reactions and three questions. The reaction usually comes; the question is the new part.
9.support: If only the reaction comes, wait. Do not continue — the silence is the prompt.
9.challenge: Give an opinion she agrees with, so she has to ask why anyway.
9.monitoring: Whether the question back comes without being cued.
9.evidence: How many of the three carried both moves.
9.transition: Move on when three questions have been asked.

10.goal: To sustain a real disagreement about a subject she chooses, for six turns, with the support closed.
10.interaction: T–S, sustained. You disagree, genuinely, and do not give in on the first argument.
run: Let her choose the subject. Give her thirty seconds and let her write two words if she wants.
Disagree with her position, and mean it. Do not concede on the first argument.
Count the turns silently. Do not correct anything, and do not fill her silences.
If she stalls twice in a row, point at the closed button, let her look, and close it again.
exact: Opening: “Tell me what you think about that. I probably disagree.”
First push back: “I do not see it. Why do you say that?”
Second push back, after her reason: “That is one reason. Is that all you have got?”
10.expected: Six turns or more. Opinion, reason, second reason under pressure, one time-buying phrase, one question back.
10.support: The moves are behind a closed button. Open only after two consecutive stalls, and close it again as soon as she looks.
10.challenge: Concede one point and immediately attack another, so she has to change tack rather than repeat herself.
10.monitoring: Count the turns. Note every silence and what she did with it. Note whether she asked you anything.
10.evidence: Number of turns without pulling; what she did in the silences; whether the question came back. This is the main record of the lesson.
10.transition: Move on after six turns, or when the subject genuinely runs out.

11.goal: To open a conversation herself, on a new subject, with nothing on the screen.
run: Read the task on screen with her: second round, new subject, and this time she opens it.
Help her land on the subject before anything starts: name two areas she has not talked about today and let her pick one.
Then hand her the turn and stop talking. The first question is hers.
Answer her questions honestly and briefly, so that she has to keep asking.
Give a reason only when she asks for it. If she does not ask, do not offer.
exact: Setting it up: “Second round, new subject — and this time you start. Ask me what I think about something, and then go after the reason.”
Choosing the subject: “Not the movie this time. Something from school, or something you have been watching.”
If the silence goes past ten seconds: “You start this one. Ask me something.”
11.expected: She opens, asks for the reason at least twice, and says what she thinks as well. Six turns.
11.support: None on screen. If she cannot start, give her the first two words of a question and stop.
11.challenge: Give a short, unhelpful answer once and let her work out that she has to ask again.
11.monitoring: Whether she asks the first question once the subject is set, without being pushed again. It is the clearest measure of initiative in this lesson.
11.evidence: Whether she started it herself, and how many times she went after the reason.
11.transition: Move on when the second conversation has run its course.

12.goal: To give one point of feedback and run the conversation again at natural pace.
run: Write one thing that worked and one thing to build on.
Put one of her sentences and a clearer version of it side by side in the boxes.
Open the replay: same subject, and this time you speak at normal speed and do not wait for her.
exact: Praising her production: “You kept that going, and you never went quiet. That is the whole point of today.”
12.expected: A shorter, faster version of the same conversation. Buying time out loud becomes necessary rather than optional here.
12.support: If she loses the turn twice, slow down once, and then go back to normal.
12.challenge: Do not pause between your turns at all.
12.monitoring: Whether the time-buying phrases survive when the pace goes up.
12.evidence: Whether the moves held at speed. It is the difference between knowing them and having them.
12.transition: Move on when the replay has run.

13.goal: To close the lesson with what was worked on and where it goes.
13.interaction: T–S, ticking the recap and the confidence scale together.
run: Go through the recap list and tick what was done.
Let her fill the confidence scale herself.
Read the three lines on the right, and say the homework out loud: notice what she says in Portuguese while she is deciding.
exact: The homework: “This week, notice what you say in Portuguese while you are thinking. There is an English one for it now.”
13.expected: Her own reading of what she can do. Listening usually comes out lower than what you saw.
13.support: If the listening mark is low, remind her what she got from one pass at normal speed on screen 4.
13.challenge: Ask which of the four time-buying phrases sounds most like her.
13.monitoring: Whether her self-assessment matches what you observed.
13.evidence: Her confidence marks, and anything she said about the pre-class.
13.transition: End here. The next lesson takes the questions she asked today and works on their order.
